title: Vidyut Jammwal: Hollywood Sets Run on Discipline, Bollywood Has Catching Up to Do
excerpt: At a Mumbai promotional event for his Hollywood debut Street Fighter, the action star said the biggest difference between Hollywood and Bollywood sets isn't budgets — it's punctuality, strict labor laws, and a 300-strong crew that never runs late.
body:
• Vidyut Jammwal, making his Hollywood debut as Dhalsim in Street Fighter (out October 16 in English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu), said the biggest difference between Hollywood and Bollywood film sets is discipline, not budgets.
  • "For the first time, I saw 300 people on set following strict discipline," he said at a Mumbai promotional event. Arriving even a minute late gets a worried call asking "whether you are in hospital."
  • He praised strict U.S. labor laws: every technician is compensated for every extra minute of overtime — "They thus wait to do overtime!"
  • Jammwal trained in Kalaripayattu since age three and was picked by a global casting agency; Star Studios 18's Ajit Andhare said "a global casting agency was searching the world and for them to have found this gem in India was something to be proud about."

Vidyut Jammwal has worked on Indian film sets for 15 years. On the Hollywood set of Street Fighter, he found a working culture he had never encountered: 300 people following strict discipline, where lateness simply does not exist.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=BhCWeWQ2aNA

"There Are Major Differences, Really Major Ones"

Asked about the working styles in India versus Hollywood, Jammwal did not mince words. "There are major differences, really major ones, and that is not about budgets, which is also true, of course," he said, according to the South Asian Herald.

https://x.com/aajtak/status/2107323355968028672

"For the first time, I saw 300 people on set following strict discipline. Over there, an actor does not know what coming late means. He is under contract and he just has to be there. There is no concept of 'Main late ho gaya (I am late today)!' Even if you are just a minute late, you can get a call asking whether you are in hospital!"

"There are major differences, really major ones, and that is not about budgets. But what I found was the massive sense of discipline!"

— Vidyut Jammwal

He named his co-stars — Jason Momoa, 50 Cent, and Cody Rhodes — as examples of high-profile actors who adhered strictly to schedules. The second difference, Jammwal said, is legal. "The laws are so strict there. If you work overtime, each technician is compensated for every minute that he works extra. They thus wait to do overtime! We can get better, but we will take a while to get there!"

The Man Behind Dhalsim

Street Fighter, directed by Kitao Sakurai, is based on the iconic Capcom video game franchise and follows Ryu and Ken Masters as they uncover a dangerous conspiracy at a high-stakes tournament. Jammwal plays Dhalsim, the yoga master whose original character can extend his limbs and breathe fire.

That casting was no accident. Jammwal has practiced the Indian martial art of Kalaripayattu since the age of three, and Star Studios 18 head Ajit Andhare made the connection explicit. "There is only one guy who can embody the character of Dhalsim, who embodies Yoga, Kalaripayyatu and Martial Arts. Guys, he is not acting, he knows all of these and that is Vidyut!"

Andhare also revealed that a global casting agency searched the world for the role before landing on Jammwal — and pointed to the lineage of Indian stars crossing over: "There was Priyanka Chopra Jonas with Baywatch, then there was Deepika Padukone with Vin Diesel and XXX, Anil Kapoor of course who has been our ambassador in MI and today we have this gentleman — Vidyut Jammwal."

Asked how the impossible moves were handled on screen, Jammwal compared the VFX work to Indian belief in mythological cinema. "What you will see on screen is exactly what you see in the game — how they look, how they fight, and what is their temperament," he said. "Impossible things done with VFX or green screen in such a way that it will all look realistic, like how we see Hanuman-ji flying holding a mountain, and we believe that is possible."

A Familiar Theme for Jammwal

This is not the first time Jammwal has spoken about the gap between Indian and international production culture. During promotions for Junglee (2019), directed by Hollywood veteran Chuck Russell — the filmmaker behind The Mask, The Scorpion King and Eraser — he praised Russell's schedule discipline and said India's filmmakers would benefit from the same rigor.

"The laws are so strict there. If you work overtime, each technician is compensated for every minute that he works extra. They thus wait to do overtime!"

— Vidyut Jammwal

What's Next

Street Fighter releases in India on October 16 in English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu — an unusually wide linguistic footprint for a Hollywood action film. The question Jammwal's remarks raise is whether Bollywood takes the message seriously: if the world's biggest-budget machine runs on punctuality, unionized overtime and contracts everyone respects, the pressure on Mumbai's production culture to evolve will only grow.
